name: embedded-value
intent: Map a value object into several columns of its owner's row instead of giving it a table of its own, so a small identity-less concept survives the relational round trip without a join, a key or a foreign key.
problem: A value object - a currency-aware money amount, a date range, an address, a coordinate - has no identity and no lifecycle of its own, so storing it as a row forces an invented key, an extra table and a join on every read. At the same time the object must not be flattened into loose primitives on the domain side: the cluster of attributes has to stay one typed concept with its invariants, and the mapper still has to write and read each of its fields. The decision is therefore where the fields go, not whether the object exists.
context: Relational stores, wherever a mapper persists an entity that holds one or more value objects. Applies when the value's fields belong together in the same row as the owner - money in an order, a period in an employment, an address in a customer - when the value is never queried on its own and never referenced by another row, and when the same value type is reused across several owners so its column layout must be reusable. The decision is taken together with the key strategy: the value contributes columns, never a key.
benefits: No invented identity and no extra table: the value's fields live in the owner's row, so loading an owner is still one row and never a join.

The domain model keeps the typed concept: money stays Money, a period stays a date range, and the validation, equality and behaviour of the value object survive persistence instead of degenerating into primitives on the owner.
Column layout is expressed once per value type: every owner that embeds the type gets the same decomposition, so the mapping knowledge is not copied into each owning class.
Round trips stay atomic: the value is written and read as part of the owner's INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT, so a partially written value cannot exist and no second write is needed for it.

Column-level constraints still apply to the value's fields - NOT NULL, CHECK, length, index - because they are ordinary columns of the owner's table, which a serialized payload in one column cannot offer.
Schema evolution is local: adding a field to the value type adds a column to the owners' tables and to the one mapping, without a new table, a new key or a new relationship.
tradeoffs: The owner's table grows: a rich value type widens the row, so tables that embed several values get many columns and every query that selects the owner pays for them.

Column names must be made unique: embedding the same value type twice (billing and shipping address) needs a prefix or explicit attribute overrides, otherwise the two instances collide on the same columns.

The value is not addressable from SQL as a unit: you cannot join to it, key it, or update 'the value' in one statement - only its individual columns, which leaks the decomposition to anyone writing queries.

The mapping is duplicated by design across owners when the value is reused: the same type embedded in five tables has its layout declared in five places (or one override per owner), and a change to the type is a change to every owner's schema.

Nullability becomes awkward: a value object whose fields are all NULL is indistinguishable from an absent value, so 'no address' and 'address with everything empty' collapse unless the mapping is given explicit rules.
The value cannot be shared or interned across rows: each owner carries its own copy of the columns, so a commonly repeated value cannot be deduplicated the way a referenced row could.

participants.responsibility: The value object being stored: identity-less, immutable or replaced as a whole, with its own invariants and equality, and no mapping knowledge of the table it lands in.
The entity whose row receives the value's columns; it holds the value as an ordinary attribute and is the only object clients load or save.

Decomposes the value into its fields on write and recomposes it on read (the classic type-converter or embedded-attribute pair); modern form: the annotation or mapping declaration that tells the ORM which columns belong to the value.
Keeps the decomposition collision-free when the same value type appears more than once in one owner, by prefixing or explicitly naming the value's columns.
Selects and filters the value's individual columns; the only place where the decomposition is visible to callers, and the reason the value stays non-addressable in SQL.

use_cases: Money amounts on orders, invoices and payments: amount plus currency stored as two columns on the order row, so Money stays a typed concept in the domain model and the currency constraint is a column-level CHECK rather than application logic.

Date ranges for employment periods, validity windows and booking intervals: a Period value object (start date, end date, possibly duration) embedded in the Employment or Booking entity, with database-level constraint that end ≥ start.

Postal addresses and contact details on customers, suppliers and shipments: multiple addresses per owner (billing, shipping, registered office) are each embedded with an explicit @AttributeOverride prefix, so all address fields coexist on the same row without collision.

Geographic coordinates, dimensions and physical measurements: a Measurement value object (numeric value, unit of measure, precision) embedded in a Product or Cargo entity, ensuring the unit travels with the value and is never accidentally omitted.

Insurance premiums, claim amounts and benefit calculations: a Money-equivalent with currency, amount and settlement-date fields embedded on the Policy or Claim entity, enabling column-level NOT NULL and CHECK constraints on the financial figures.

Patient vitals and clinical measurements in healthcare systems: a VitalReading value object (value, unit, capture-timestamp, device-id) embedded in an Encounter or Observation entity, with the unit of measure encoded alongside the value so no ambiguity exists across international deployments.

Order-line price breakdowns in e-commerce: unit price, tax amount, discount amount and currency each live as columns on the order-line row, keeping the pricing calculation auditable and queryable at the column level rather than hidden in a serialized payload.
Audit timestamps and changelog entries: an AuditRecord value object (who, when, which version) embedded in entities that need lightweight audit metadata without a separate audit-log table join.

Sensor readings with calibration metadata in IoT platforms: a CalibratedMeasurement value object (raw value, calibrated value, unit, calibration-date) embedded in a SensorReading entity, stored alongside the owning sensor's row for co-located access.

Reusable name, code and identifier value types shared across many entities: a natural-key identifier (scheme, value, label) embedded wherever it appears, with one declaration of the three-column layout that every owner reuses.

Legacy wide tables that must map onto a clean domain model: a denormalised legacy schema is wrapped with embeddables that restore the typed concept, allowing a clean object model without introducing new tables.

Doctrine ORM embeddables: a User entity embeds an Address value object whose street, postal code, city and country are inlined as user-table columns with a configurable prefix (address_ by default, customizable or disabled via columnPrefix), and DQL filters on u.address.city as if it were a native field.

EF Core 8+ complex types: an Address or Coordinate value object declared with ComplexProperty is stored inline in the owner's table via table splitting, or as a single JSON column, with copy-by-value semantics and full ExecuteUpdate support - the recommended successor to owned entities for identity-free value objects.

Jakarta Persistence 3.2 embeddables: a Java record annotated @Embeddable is stored as an intrinsic part of the owning entity and shares its identity, making immutable record-based value types first-class embedded values under the specification itself.
avoid_when: The value is referenced from other rows or needs its own identity - map it as an entity with Identity Field and Foreign Key Mapping instead.
The value is queried, joined or aggregated in SQL on its own, or must be addressable as a unit - a table of its own, or Serialized LOB plus an indexed projection, fits better.
The value graph is deep, unbounded or likely to change shape often - Serialized LOB in one column avoids a schema migration per change.
The value is really a collection (a list of addresses, a set of phone numbers) - a collection of embeddables in a dependent table, or Dependent Mapping, is the honest mapping.
The owner already carries so many columns that a wide row is the problem - a separate table may be worth the join.
The store is a document database and the value is naturally a nested document: embedding is then a store decision, not a relational mapping decision.
anti_patterns: Giving the value its own table, key and foreign key 'for cleanliness', then joining on every load to fetch a date range: the identity and the join the pattern exists to avoid.
Embedding a value that is really an entity (own lifecycle, referenced from elsewhere), so two rows hold divergent copies of what should be one row.
Serialising the value into one column and calling it embedded: no constraints, no partial predicates, and every change to the value's shape becomes an unversioned payload migration.
Embedding a collection by numbering the columns (phone1, phone2, phone3): the schema now encodes an arbitrary bound and the domain loses the collection.
Letting the owner's class expose the value's individual columns as its own attributes, so the value object exists only in the mapping and not in the model.
Using one flat set of value columns for two different values in the same row (amount/currency for both net and gross), so the second value overwrites the first on every save.
design_principles: Values are not entities: no identity, no lifecycle of their own, therefore no key and no table.
Single source of truth for the mapping: the decomposition of a value type is declared once and reused by every owner.
Encapsulation: the owner exposes the value object, never its individual fields, so the concept cannot be partially set from outside.
Separation of concerns: the value carries domain rules, the mapper carries column names - neither knows the other's business.
Prefer composition over inheritance: reuse of a column group comes from embedding a value type, not from a superclass with the same fields.
best_practices: Decide the value/entity split first: if the concept needs a key, is referenced from another row, or has its own lifecycle, do not embed it — map it as an entity with Identity Field and Foreign Key Mapping instead.

Name each embedding explicitly: use @AttributeOverride (JPA), HasColumnName (EF Core), or composite column aliases (SQLAlchemy) so the same value type embedded twice in one owner gets distinct columns — a silent collision is a data-corruption bug.

Keep the embeddable immutable (or replace it as a whole): the mapper always writes a complete decomposition and never a partial update, which preserves consistency and avoids read-before-write patterns.

Declare the null rule explicitly: either all of the value's columns are NULLABLE and an all-NULL row means 'absent', or the columns are NOT NULL and the value is mandatory — encode it in the mapper and document it in the embeddable class.

Add column constraints at the embeddable level (NOT NULL, CHECK, length, precision) rather than in the mapper: this is the pattern's main advantage over Serialized LOB and ensures constraints are enforced regardless of which owner writes the value.

When the ORM has a declarative form (@Embeddable, ComplexProperty, composite()), declare the decomposition there and let schema generation, migrations and query building share the single declaration — never duplicate the layout in each owner.

For EF Core 11+: prefer ComplexProperty (complex types) for value objects stored inline; only use OwnsOne/OwnsMany (owned entities) when the storage genuinely requires a separate table or a separate-tracking identity.

Ensure the embeddable overrides equals() and hashCode() on all fields (or on a business-key subset): two value instances with identical fields must compare equal, and Hibernate/SQLAlchemy use these for identity within a session.

Avoid embedding unbounded collections: a list of addresses, line items or phone numbers is a separate association, not a value — use a dependent table or OwnsMany, not a fixed set of numbered columns (phone1, phone2, …).

Validate embeddable invariants at construction time: if a Money amount must be non-negative or a postal code must match a country, enforce it in the value object's constructor, not in the owner's business logic — the embeddable must be safe to construct without a database connection.

Use a consistent column-naming convention across the codebase: attribute_name.column_name (e.g., billing_address_city, shipping_address_city) so developers can predict the schema layout without consulting the mapper.

When the embedded type contains a nested embeddable, apply the same explicit-override discipline at every level and keep the full attribute path in the column name (e.g., home_address_zip_code_postal).
Avoid embedding when the value type is queried, aggregated, or joined independently in SQL: a separate table with a key fits better — the embedded form is invisible to SQL as a unit.

Test the decomposition in both directions: write an owner, fetch it back, mutate only the embedded value, write again and assert the other owner columns are unchanged — catches missing mapper configuration early.
Document the embeddable's column layout in its class Javadoc or docstring: every owner reusing the type should have a single authoritative source for the column names, not a reverse-engineered guess.

related_patterns_notes.value-object: the domain concept that Embedded Value persists; a value object is identity-less, immutable and compared by attribute, and Embedded Value is the persistence-side expression of that contract.
related_patterns_notes.identity-field: the pattern a value object explicitly does NOT need; a value object has no key and no table, so Identity Field is irrelevant for it but relevant for the entities that own it.
related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: the layer that typically performs the decompose/recompose work; the mapper reads the embeddable's fields and writes them as owner columns, and reverses that on loading.
related_patterns_notes.foreign-key-mapping: the pattern Embedded Value avoids; when a value is given a key and a table and a foreign-key reference, it has become an entity, not an embedded value.
related_patterns_notes.serialized-lob: the fallback when the value's shape changes often or the columns would be too many; Serialized LOB stores the value in one column, giving flexibility at the cost of column-level constraints and SQL queryability.
related_patterns_notes.dependent-mapping: the pattern for mapping a collection of value objects that are owned by one entity and stored in a dependent table; distinct from Embedded Value which stores inline with the owner row.
related_patterns_notes.composite-entity: an entity whose data spans multiple database rows linked by a common key; unlike an embedded value, a composite entity has identity and its own lifecycle, making it a heavier construct.
related_patterns_notes.class-table-inheritance: a inheritance strategy that maps each subclass to its own table; value objects embedded within a class-table hierarchy still live in the owner's columns, not in the subclass table.
related_patterns_notes.attribute-override: the JPA annotation (@AttributeOverride) that resolves column-name collisions when the same embeddable type is used more than once in one entity; a key enabling practice for the pattern.
related_patterns_notes.table-splitting: an EF Core technique where multiple entity types share the same primary table; used with owned entities to co-locate owned-type columns on the owner's row.
